key_insight: System-level defenses—combining dynamic, policy-aware planning with contextual isolation and provenance—can substantially reduce the risk that maliciously embedded instructions in untrusted inputs (indirect prompt injection) will cause harmful agent behavior.
problem_solved: Protects AI agents (LLM-driven) from indirect prompt injection attacks, where malicious instructions hidden in external data can hijack agent goals or capabilities and trigger unsafe actions.
method: Design agent architectures that support dynamic replanning and runtime security-policy updates so agents adapt safely in changing environments.
Apply contextual isolation and least-privilege execution (sandboxing, capability-limited modules) to prevent untrusted inputs from influencing critical decision paths.
Add provenance, input validation, verification checkpoints, and human-in-the-loop gating for high-risk actions to trace and block injected instructions.
impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners concrete, system-level design principles to integrate security into agent workflows—reducing attack surface and improving reliability in realistic, dynamic deployments.
visual_elements: Architecture diagram: agent pipeline showing trusted vs untrusted data flows, policy enforcement points, and sandboxed modules.
Sequence/timeline: dynamic replanning loop with checkpoints for policy updates and human-in-the-loop interventions.
Before/after comparison: attack scenario (prompt injection leads to unsafe action) versus defended scenario (isolation + provenance prevents action).
Icon set: sandbox, shield (policy), fingerprint (provenance), and human-in-loop to denote defense building blocks.
paper_title: Architecting Secure AI Agents: Perspectives on System-Level Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
paper_authors: Chong Xiang, Drew Zagieboylo, Shaona Ghosh, Sanjay Kariyappa, Kai Greshake
